claims.text: The low-dimensional state of as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi films and nanoribbons produces enhanced surface and interface disorder.
Surface and interface disorder increases magnetic domain-wall pinning.
Surface and interface disorder increases spin misalignment.
Disorder-induced domain-wall pinning and spin misalignment suppress the magnetocaloric response.
Disorder-induced domain-wall pinning and spin misalignment enlarge magnetic hysteresis.
Heat-transfer limitations further impair the magnetic-cooling response at higher cycling frequencies.
The deposition process produces crystallographic defects and surface or interface disorder in the FeMnNiGeSi films and ribbons.
Deposition methods can fabricate sub-10 nm multicomponent nanoalloys.
Controlled low-temperature annealing is the proposed intervention for reducing surface and interface disorder while avoiding significant phase transformation.
Annealing will reduce defect density and improve crystallinity in the FeMnNiGeSi nanoscale samples.
Reduced disorder and defect density will enhance magnetic ordering.
Reduced disorder and defect density will lower the energy barriers for domain-wall motion.
Improved structural order will produce a sharper magnetic phase transition.
Annealing-induced structural improvement will improve heat transfer during cooling cycles.
Annealed samples will exhibit a greater isothermal entropy change than as-deposited controls under identical low-field conditions.
Annealed samples will exhibit narrower magnetic hysteresis loops than as-deposited controls under identical low-field conditions.
The proposed operating regime is sub-10 nm sample thickness, applied magnetic fields below 0.5 T, and cycling frequencies below the platform's heat-transfer limit.
A failure to obtain both a statistically significant magnetocaloric increase and a hysteresis-width decrease after annealing would falsify the hypothesis.
